content.title: Review for "Graph Adversarial Networks"
content.review:
****Summary****

This paper proposed to defend against the information leaking in the graph node embedding. The ‘adversarial attack’ in the title is not with the commonly used sense, but is talking about identifying certain sensitive attributes from the embedding representation. The authors came up with a minimax formulation, where the ‘primal’ GNN tries to learn a good embedding for the downstream classification task, while also avoiding leaking sensitive attribute information. The ‘dual’ model tries to tell the sensitive attribute from the embedding. The author shows some claims on the tradeoff between these two objectives, and has carried out extensive experiments on graph datasets to verify the idea.

****Pros****

- The paper is well written and easy to follow. 
- The theoretical claims on the tradeoff between predictive performance and ‘safety’ is interesting. 
- The experiments are relatively comprehensive.

****Cons****

- The problem might not be very practical, and the usage of adversarial attack might be confusing.
- There’s little technical contribution or innovation.
- There might be flaws in the experimental design.


****Overall I lean towards rejection****. Please see my detailed comments below:

- The major issue with this paper is the validness of its problem definition. This problem assumes that one can get access to the latent embedding representation of some deployed system, which is not quite practical. If the hacker is able to obtain such embedding, then it would be more direct to hack the database to get the sensitive information. Note that this is different from the classical adversarial attack, where one can make tweaks on the images, or in the graph domain where one can deliberately create/delete friendship to modify the graphs. The adversarial attack is an issue, as one can easily modify the inputs to try to fool the blackbox system. However I’m not fully convinced that the problem studied in this paper is valuable. 

- The technical contribution is mainly coming from the Eq (4), which is a standard objective in many adversarial learning works. The theoretical results are interesting, which show the trade-off between the two objectives mathematically. However, this is also limited to this specific problem proposed, and it didn’t give a practical solution on how to choose the best \lambda (or maybe we don’t have a definition of the ‘best’). 

- I would suggest to avoid using the phrase ‘adversarial attack’, as it has its well recognized definition. The problem studied here is closer to the ‘privacy’ or ‘information leaking’. 

- One detail that might be missing is: whether the ‘attacker’ performance is obtained by the attacker that is directly trained in the minimax objective from Eq (4), or is it performed after Eq (4) is fully trained, and train a new attacker that uses embeddings from GNN and attribute labels from the training data? The concern with the former one is that the Eq (4) might reach some trivial equilibrium. 

- Regarding the neighborhood attack, what will happen if the attacker in Eq (4) is trained only with the node embedding information (without neighborhood gathering), and after that we train a separate attacker that leverages neighborhood information to infer the sensitive attribute? 

- Similarly to above, can we have a flexible form of adversarial f in Eq (4), such that after training, it would be robust to different parameterizations of the attacker that is trained with/without neighborhood information? As it is also hard to assume the specific model the attacker would use, the Eq (4) should be general enough to capture the worst f in the family. 


****Questions****

I’d like to hear the answers to all my questions above. 


****How to improve****

Actually I feel the problem in machine learning fairness might be more relevant. Instead of formulating the problem as protecting from adversarial attackers, it would be better and more natural/useful to formulate it as a ‘fair’ classifier that shouldn’t make decisions on top of the sensitive attributes. There are several definitions in the fairness domain, like equalized odds, that might be relevant to Eq (2).
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Our response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for the valuable feedback. We hope to take this chance to clarify the misconception in the review.

**Q**: “validness of problem definition”

A: As the reviewer has already pointed out, our threat model is different from the adversarial attack in robustness and the link modification on graph edges. In particular, under our threat model, the attacker will have access to the GNN node representations before the last year, and he would like to infer sensitive attributes from these representations. Such an attack scenario is ubiquitous in client-server paradigm, where the centralized machine learning server is provided as a service (MLaaS) to all the end nodes. In this case, each node in GNN corresponds to an end user and the encoder corresponds to a local sensitive information filter embedded on a local device. An attacker in this case tries to eavesdrop the network traffic data in order to steal sensitive information from end users, but such data have already been processed by the local filters. Note that it is much harder for an attacker to hack each local device directly than eavesdropping the traffic data in the client-server model.

**Q**: “how to choose the best lambda”

A: As the reviewer has already realized, there is no “best” choice of lambda, since each lambda defines a different trade-off between accuracy and privacy. In other words, choosing different lambdas corresponds to placing different points on the Pareto frontier between accuracy and privacy, so it is really up to the users who need to specify the value of lambda, depending on the concrete application problems they’re facing. 

**Q**: “avoid using adversarial attacks”

A: Thanks for the suggestion, but we’d like to point out that privacy is often reserved for the notion of differential privacy, and this is precisely the reason why we tried to avoid using “privacy” throughout the paper to avoid the potential confusion and misunderstanding. We agree that the term “adversarial attacks” is used more often in the literature of adversarial robustness. In light of both concerns, we are happy to use the term “information leakage”.

**Q**: Which attacker is used?

A: Note that the attacker is a worst-case attacker trained from the training set by optimizing Eq. (4) directly. So as long as the test data comes from the same distribution as the training data, in principle this shouldn’t make a difference. Of course, we agree that due to the complication of optimizing a non-convex-non-concave minimax game, this is no guarantee that a good equilibrium is reached. 

**Q**: What if trained with node embedding but attack with neighborhood gathering?

A: The idea is that the defense will be less effective than training a worst-case attacker with access to neighborhood-level information in Eq (4). We explored a different perspective on the effect of neighborhood aggregation on defense in Figure 3, and we are happy to provide additional experiments regarding this scenario if required.

**Q**: Robust to different parameterization? 

A: We’d like to point out that the formulation in Eq.(4) is indeed a worst-case scenario, i.e., the min part is to find an encoder that is robust to the worst possible attacker from a certain family $F_A$. Furthermore, the security guarantee in Theorem 3 is also information-theoretic, meaning that there is no assumption on the attacker $f$. However, this only applies to attack without neighborhood gathering. 

We thank the reviewer’s suggestion on the connection of our work to fairness. Indeed, it’s similar to the so-called demographic parity in the fair ML literature, but we also feel our formulation of the problem using attacks (or information leakage as suggested) is more relevant, given its potentially wide applications in client-server model where ML is provided as a service.

content.title: Follow-up
content.comment: Has our response addressed all your concerns? Let us know if you have more questions. Thank you!

content.title: Interesting attack on graph data but misses related work on data privacy
content.review:
This paper studies the problem of attribute inference attack on graphs with GNNs and proposes an adversarial training framework (minmax game) to maximize accuracy while minimizing information leakage about sensitive attributes.  

Pros: 
The paper is very well written and studies an interesting attack problem on graph data. 

Cons: 
-	Attack setup is not clear. It is assumed that the attacker has access to the GNN’s representation before the last layer and wants to guess the sensitive attribute. This particular attack model needs to be motivated as it’s not clear from the paper what real-world scenario it targets.
-	Similar attack setting has been indeed considered in many recent papers in context of data privacy [1-8], with most considering the use-case of private inference with network partitioned between a client and a server. Many papers have adopted adversarial training framework, and some have presented information theoretic analysis as well. 
-	So, while attribute inference attacks on graph data is an important problem, the novelty of the proposed method is limited as it seems previous approaches can be directly used on graph data and with GNNs as well. In fact, for the most part, it seems the proposed method in the paper is not specific to graph data and GNNs either. So, the paper must discuss in what aspects it is different from the prior art and how the proposed method compares with existing methods. 

References: 

[1] Edwards and Storkey, “Censoring Representations with an Adversary”

[2] Jihun Hamm, “Minimax Filter: Learning to Preserve Privacy from Inference Attacks”

[3] Li et al., “PrivyNet: A Flexible Framework for Privacy-Preserving Deep Neural Network Training”

[4] Xie, et al., “Controllable Invariance through Adversarial Feature Learning”

[5] Song and Shmatikov, “Overlearning Reveals Sensitive Attributes”

Also on text data:

[6] Elazar and Goldberg, “Adversarial Removal of Demographic Attributes from Text Data”

[7] Coavoux, et al., “Privacy-preserving Neural Representations of Text Maximin”

[8] Li et al., “Towards Robust and Privacy-preserving Text Representations”

content.title: Our response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback.

**Q**: “Attack setup”

A: Indeed, our threat model is that the attacker will have access to the GNN node representations before the last layer, and they would like to infer sensitive attributes from these representations. Such an attack scenario is ubiquitous in client-server paradigm, where the centralized machine learning server is provided as a service (MLaaS) to all the end nodes. In this case, each node in GNN corresponds to an end user and the encoder corresponds to a local sensitive information filter embedded in the local device. An attacker tries to steal sensitive data through network traffic, but such data have already been processed by the local filters.

**Q**: “Similar attack setting...”

A: To the best of our knowledge, all the works [1-8] either consider image data or text data, whereas our work mainly focuses on graph-structured data, which is different from all these previous works. The unique node representation propagation scheme in GNNs makes the underlying optimization problem particularly challenging in our case, which does not appear in previous works. We are happy to provide more discussions and comparisons to these prior works.

content.title: Concerns not addressed
content.comment: Unfortunately the response does not fully address the concerns. I think the problem studied is fundamentally the same as the split learning framework used for private edge-server inference and should be placed as such. There are many papers that studied the privacy problem in this context and developed similar techniques and theories for minimizing information leakage about sensitive attributes. I agree this paper is different in that it works on graph data, but the data type does not seem to fundamentally change the problem. The authors need to discuss the related work in depth (even if those papers do not consider graph data) and detail the technical novelty of their proposed method.

content.title: Comparison with related work missing
content.review:
Summary: The paper proposes a defense against attribute inference attacks on graphs. The defense is formulated as a minimax game where the defender aims to learn node representations that do not contain information about a given sensitive attribute, while the attacker aims to maximize the contained information. The authors prove a lower bound for the inference error (w.r.t. the sensitive attribute) that any attacker has to incur. They also discuss the loss in accuracy if the adversarial advantage is minimized and the conclusions depend on the correlation between the target and the sensitive attribute.

Reasons for score: The score of 5 is mainly due to a lack of comparison with related work in the evaluation and the similarity of the theoretical contributions with previous work (see weak points). If the authors include a more comprehensive empirical evaluation and clearly delineate the relation to previous work I am willing to increase my score.

Strong points:
* The theoretical characterization of the inference error and the loss in accuracy is useful (despite strong assumptions)
* The detailed evaluation in terms of \lambda and n-hop, as well as the comparison between node and neighbor attacks in insightful.
* Studying attribute inference attacks on graphs is important and has not been tackled so far.

Weak points:
* Similar (or equivalent) theoretical contributions have been presented in [1] (accepted to NeurIPS 2020, initially submitted on ArXiv on 19.06.2019), compare e.g. Theorem 3 here to Theorem 3.1 in [1]. The difference to this prior work should be clearly stated. Moreover, the analysis does not exploit the fact that the encoder is a GNN. 
* There is no comparison to other approaches for (adversarial) removal of sensitive/protected attributes or approaches for learning fair representations (e.g. [2, 3, 4, 5] to mention just a few), except the single comparison to (Bose & Hamilton, 2019). See also questions.
* There is no evaluation for the popular task of node classification, only link prediction and graph regression. 

Question for the authors:
1. How does the proposed approach compare to other approaches for (adversarial) removal of sensitive/protected attributes (see weak points)?
2. Why is the comparison to (Bose & Hamilton, 2019) only presented for ML-1M and not for the other datasets? Note that (Bose & Hamilton, 2019) also show results on FB15K-237 in their work.
3. Often the sensitive attribute has a skewed distribution (e.g. majority vs. minority) in practice. How does the proposed approach perform in such settings? In particular, does the performance for the minority class suffer more than the majority class?
4. How does your approach perform for other (general) architectures and tasks? (since the method is agnostic to the encoder function, see also weak points)
5. Does the theory apply to the setting of multiple sensitive attributes? (I acknowledge the empirical results on FB15K-237)

Additional feedback that did not affect the decision:
* The encoder g can be held fixed (e.g. after pretraining along with h). In the current experiments pretraining is done, but g is not fixed. How does the proposed approach perform if g is fixed and only h and f are optimized? What does this setup imply for the derived guarantees? 
* Can the requirement that "the task classifier and the adversary have unlimited capacity" be relaxed? In particular, can we take into account the set of functions representable by GNNs with a small number of layers as used in pratice?
* It would be interesting to evaluate whether the proposed approach is effective at defending against edge attribute inference (including the existence of an edge).
* It would be interesting to study how does a homophily (or heterophily) assumption change the problem in theory and practice. For example, experiments on data generated from an SBM model with different parameters might be insightful. 

Typos:
* supresum 
* transformation to removing information

##  After Rebuttal
After reading the rest of the reviews and the authors' response I have decided to keep the score.

It is not clear why the techniques in [2-5] (or the techniques in the references given by Reviewer 4) cannot be applied on graphs since at least some of these formulations appear to be model/task agnostic. I would suggest either including a comparison or making a stronger case why a comparison is not possible.

References:
1. Zhao, Han, Jianfeng Chi, Yuan Tian, and Geoffrey J. Gordon. "Trade-offs and Guarantees of Adversarial Representation Learning for Information Obfuscation"
2. Elazar, Yanai, and Yoav Goldberg. "Adversarial removal of demographic attributes from text data."
3. Roy, Proteek Chandan, and Vishnu Naresh Boddeti. "Mitigating information leakage in image representations: A maximum entropy approach."
4. Xie, Qizhe, Zihang Dai, Yulun Du, Eduard Hovy, and Graham Neubig. "Controllable invariance through adversarial feature learning."
5. Louizos, Christos, Kevin Swersky, Yujia Li, Max Welling, and Richard Zemel. "The variational fair autoencoder."

replying_to: Replying to Comparison with related work missing

content.title: Our response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable insights and constructive comments. 

**Q**: Relation to prior works

A: Thanks! We are happy to provide more discussions with [1]. Indeed, since both Theorem 3.1 in [1] and Theorem 3 in this work are information-theoretic results, they hold for all the possible encoders, including GNN encoders as well. Restricting to GNN encoders will only lead to a smaller lower bound in this case. The difference of Theorem 3 here is that we’re free of the $I(\hat{A}; A | Z) = 0$ assumption. 

**Q**: Comparison to [2, 3, 4, 5]

A: As the reviewer has realized and mentioned “Studying attribute inference attacks on graphs is important and has not been tackled so far.”, none of [2-5] is proposed on graph-structured data. In fact, proposing the adversarial defense technique on graph-structured data is one of our key contributions. Furthermore, it is not clear techniques in [2-5] could be straightforwardly applied on graphs. 

**Q**: No node classification task

A: For node classification, we qualitatively evaluated the performance of GAL on the Cora dataset in Figure 2. 

**Q**: Comparison with (Bose & Hamilton, 2019) on FB15K-237

A: (Bose & Hamilton, 2019)’s experimental setup on FB15k-237 differs from that of our work: instead of attacking individual attributes, in our work the attacks are performed on all 50 attributes at once, so the results are not comparable. 

**Q**: Skewed sensitive distribution

A: For extremely imbalanced sensitive distribution, it is clear that even a naive attacker could achieve high attack accuracy by guessing the majority label. In this case the max part of Eq. (4) will have less effect on the learning of GNN encoder, so we won’t lose much task accuracy. But on the other hand, this also means that the defense is less effective, which is expected. From an optimization perspective, this is due to the fact that the loss of the max part can easily plateau, hence the gradient from the max part will essentially vanish.

**Q**: Other architectures and tasks

A: Note that we have experimented with *extensive* GNN encoders, and the results on these various GNN encoders are consistent. We believe our framework could also be easily extended to other GNN architectures as well, since our formulation and analysis is essentially encoder-agnostic. 

**Q**: Extension to multiple sensitive attribute

A: Yes, and this is straightforward. To see this, given k sensitive attributes, say, $A_1, …, A_k$, we could easily reduce this multiple sensitive attribute problem into our existing setting by defining $A = A_1 \otimes A_2 … \otimes A_k$ to be the Cartesian product of these k attributes. 

**Q**: Other comments and typos

A: Thanks for pointing out! We are happy to incorporate these comments to our updated version.

content.title: A good paper but not very clear
content.review:
This paper studied a problem to present information leaking from GNN embeddings. To achieve goal, they proposed a minimax game learning framework between desired GNN encoder and the attacker. The proposed method seems sound and the experimental results are provided to demonstrate the performance. 

Pros: 
1. The problem studied here seems new. There are very few papers studying this setting. 
2. The proposed solution has theoretical guarantee. 
3. The extensive set of experiments are provided to show the effectiveness. 

Cons: 
1. I think the paper title is very misleading. It looks like it studied a generic problem on graph adversarial examples. However it is actually focusing on the differential privacy problem for GNNs.   
2. The proposed algorithm has little details so it is hard to follow why this algorithm is presented to solve the problem and how to exactly solve the problem. 
3. The experimental results are not very clear. What's the measurements for different T and A? How does it measure the performance? The smaller the better? 
4. There is no computational analysis about the proposed algorithm. How efficient is the algorithm?

replying_to: Replying to A good paper but not very clear

content.title: Our response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback and constructive comments.  We would like to take this chance to clarify the misconception in the review.

1. It is true that our paper tackles a privacy problem, but the kind of privacy discussed in this paper is fundamentally different from the notion of differential privacy (DP). We have provided discussion related to DP in the Related Work section, at the end of page 2. To summarize, DP aims at defending the so-called membership inference attack [3], which aims to find randomized algorithms so that the adversary cannot guess whether an individual appears in the training data or not by looking at the output of the algorithm. In contrast, our work is concerned with attribute inference attack which aims to find transformations of the data, so that the adversary cannot guess a specific attribute value of the data. 

[3]. Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models, Shokri et al., S\&P 2017.

2. Due to the space limit, we provided detailed descriptions about our algorithmic implementation in Appendix B. 

3. Details about measurements of T and A can be found in Table 1, as well as Appendix B.  In short, for metrics like AUC, Macro-F1, MRR and Hits@10, a higher value indicates a better performance; while for metrics like MAE and RMSE, a lower value indicates a better performance.

4. The minimax framework we provided in this work is flexible and can be applied with various GNN encoders. This also means that the efficiency of the algorithm depends on the type of encoders and decoders each specific algorithmic instantiation uses. In summary, for each iteration of the optimization algorithm, the computational complexity is linear in the size of the encoder, decoder, as well as the adversarial network.
